text: National Weather Service Birmingham’s storm survey for the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado on April 27, 2011 describes a long-track, strong tornado affecting Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties in central Alabama. The survey rates the tornado as EF-3, with estimated maximum winds of 145 mph, a path length of 72.13 miles, and a maximum width of 1760 yards (about 1 mile). It reports 50 injuries and 7 fatalities. The tornado is documented as beginning in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive around 5:30 pm at coordinates 32.6152 / -88.0543 and ending near Marvel in Bibb County around 6:55 pm at 33.1524 / -86.9898. The narrative states that the tornado’s damage intensity increased along its path: it started as EF-1 in Greene County, strengthened to EF-2 there, then intensified to EF-3 north of Sawyerville in Hale County near Alabama Route 14 with 145 mph winds, causing extensive structural damage, numerous destroyed mobile and single-family homes, damage to at least one church, thousands of downed trees, about 40 injuries, and 6 fatalities in that area. The tornado crossed multiple roads and communities, including County Roads 18, 21, and 29, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and areas east of Ingram, and then moved into the Talladega National Forest producing significant tree damage up to the Bibb County line. Continuing northeast, it moved through Eoline in Bibb County, where EF-3-level structural damage occurred, destroying numerous mobile homes, single-family homes, the Eoline Fire Department, and another business; a vehicle-related fatality and at least 10 injuries occurred near Eoline. The survey notes that the tornado weakened to EF-2 with 125 mph winds as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton near County Road 26, where several structures sustained major damage or were destroyed, then continued to weaken and lifted just northeast of Marvel. The report emphasizes that tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties from 4:50 pm until 7:45 pm and includes links to radar imagery and other supporting graphics.

The National Weather Service Birmingham’s “Historic Outbreak of April 27, 2011” page summarizes a major tornado outbreak that affected central Alabama as part of a broader multi-day severe weather episode from April 25–28, 2011 across the eastern United States. It characterizes the event as historic in scope and impact, provides an event summary for central Alabama, and includes tabular listings of the many tornadoes that occurred in the Birmingham County Warning Area, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado. The overview describes that this outbreak was associated with a large-scale weather system that produced numerous strong and violent tornadoes over several days, and it links to additional resources, including a NOAA GeoPlatform page dedicated to April 27, 2011 in Alabama. The page offers contextual statistics and descriptions of the overall number, strength, and distribution of tornadoes in central Alabama during the outbreak, situating individual events like the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado within the broader regional sequence of storms.

The National Weather Service Mobile/Pensacola’s page on the April 27, 2011 tornado outbreak describes a major tornado outbreak across the Deep South that took place during a three-day period from April 25–28, 2011. It notes that this outbreak was one of the largest, deadliest, and most destructive tornado outbreaks in U.S. history. The page states that there were 343 tornadoes over the three days, with 207 tornadoes occurring on April 27 alone, and that four of the April 27 tornadoes reached EF-5 intensity. It explains that only one of the 207 tornadoes occurred within the Mobile/Pensacola County Warning Area on April 27, an EF-3 that crossed into northwestern Choctaw County, Alabama. The page references Storm Prediction Center severe weather archives and supercell rotation track analyses from the National Severe Storms Laboratory to illustrate the geographic extent of the outbreak and how far south the tornado-producing storms extended. It provides a detailed case study of the Northern Choctaw County EF-3 tornado, including its timing, path across multiple NWS County Warning Areas, track length of about 23.7 miles, and maximum winds of approximately 150 mph, highlighting how long-lived supercells produced multiple strong and violent tornadoes over a wide region.

The Wikipedia article on the 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado describes a large, long-tracked, destructive EF3 tornado that moved across central Alabama on the afternoon of April 27, 2011. It states that the tornado traveled about 72.1 miles, affecting areas near towns such as Tishabee, Sawyerville, Havana, and Eoline. The article situates this tornado within what it calls the largest tornado outbreak in modern history and includes sections on meteorological synopsis, a detailed tornado summary, and references to National Weather Service pages, Storm Prediction Center data, and news reports. As a secondary, collaboratively edited source, it synthesizes information from multiple primary references rather than providing original observational data.

statement: The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado of April 27, 2011 was rated EF-3 with estimated maximum winds of about 145 mph, a path length of approximately 72.13 miles, and a maximum width of about 1760 yards, resulting in 50 injuries and 7 fatalities as it tracked across Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties in Alabama.

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado developed in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River west of Tishabee around 5:30 pm, intensified to EF-3 north of Sawyerville in Hale County, then continued through the Talladega National Forest into Bibb County where it caused EF-3 damage in Eoline before weakening to EF-2 near Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton and dissipating just northeast of Marvel by about 6:55 pm.

Near Sawyerville in Hale County, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado intensified to EF-3 strength as it crossed Alabama Route 14, producing extensive structural damage, destroying numerous mobile and single-family homes and at least one church, downing thousands of trees, and causing roughly 40 injuries and 6 fatalities.

In Eoline in Bibb County, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado produced EF-3-caliber structural damage with estimated winds near 145 mph, destroying about a dozen mobile homes and single-family homes and demolishing the Eoline Fire Department and another business, causing one fatality in a vehicle near the fire department and at least 10 additional injuries.
Tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties from approximately 4:50 pm to 7:45 pm during the period that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred.

The April 27, 2011 tornado outbreak in central Alabama was part of a larger severe weather episode from April 25 to 28, 2011 that affected the eastern half of the United States and produced numerous tornadoes across the Birmingham County Warning Area, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado.

The three-day tornado outbreak from April 25–28, 2011 produced approximately 343 tornadoes in the United States, including about 207 tornadoes on April 27 alone, four of which reached EF-5 intensity, making the event one of the largest, deadliest, and most destructive tornado outbreaks in U.S. history.

Within the National Weather Service Mobile/Pensacola County Warning Area, only one of the 207 tornadoes on April 27, 2011 occurred, an EF-3 tornado that crossed into northern Choctaw County, Alabama, had a continuous track of about 23.7 miles, and reached maximum winds near 150 mph while spanning three different NWS County Warning Areas.

The 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is characterized as a large, long-tracked, destructive EF3 tornado that traveled roughly 72.1 miles across central Alabama on the afternoon of April 27, 2011, affecting areas near Tishabee, Sawyerville, Havana, and Eoline as part of a major tornado outbreak.

title: Overview
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was a large, long-tracked, destructive EF3 tornado that occurred during the afternoon and early evening of April 27, 2011, as part of a major tornado outbreak affecting the eastern half of the United States from April 25 to 28, 2011. [1][2][3]

According to a post-event survey by the National Weather Service (NWS) office in Birmingham, Alabama, the tornado was rated EF-3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with estimated maximum winds of about 145 mph (233 km/h), a total path length of approximately 72.13 miles (116.1 km), and a maximum width of about 1,760 yards (1.0 mile). It resulted in 7 fatalities and 50 injuries as it moved across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties in central Alabama. [1]

The tornado affected multiple rural communities and small towns along its track, including areas near Tishabee and Forkland in Greene County, Sawyerville and nearby communities in Hale County, and the community of Eoline and surrounding areas in Bibb County. [1]

Within the broader context of the April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was one of numerous significant tornadoes that occurred on April 27, 2011, a day on which about 207 tornadoes were confirmed nationwide and four reached EF5 intensity, contributing to what has been described by the National Weather Service as one of the largest, deadliest, and most destructive tornado outbreaks in United States history. [2][3]

title: Meteorological background and warning process
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado formed during a multi-day severe weather episode from April 25 to 28, 2011, during which a powerful storm system produced a widespread tornado outbreak across the eastern half of the United States. [2][3]

Across central Alabama, the NWS Birmingham office documented an extensive outbreak of tornadoes on April 27, 2011, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, as part of this larger synoptic-scale event. [2]

Based on the Birmingham storm survey, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado developed in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River, just west of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive, around 5:30 p.m. Central Daylight Time, and tracked generally northeastward for over an hour before dissipating just northeast of Marvel in Bibb County by about 6:55 p.m. CDT. [1]

The NWS Birmingham report states that tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties from approximately 4:50 p.m. until 7:45 p.m. CDT, covering the period during which the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was on the ground. [1]

title: Tornado path and intensity
content:
According to the NWS Birmingham storm survey, the tornado initially produced EF1 damage after touching down near the Tombigbee River in far southwest Greene County and moving northeast across rural portions of Greene County north of Forkland, before intensifying to EF2 intensity while still in Greene County. [1]

The tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and entered Hale County west of Sawyerville, then crossed Alabama Route 14 just north of Sawyerville, where surveyors concluded that it intensified to EF3 strength with estimated winds of 145 mph. [1]

Continuing northeast, the tornado moved across County Road 18, County Road 21, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram in Hale County, maintaining EF3 strength and producing extensive structural damage in these areas. [1]

The storm survey indicates that the tornado then entered the Talladega National Forest near Ingram and tracked northeastward toward the Bibb County line, where it caused significant tree damage along its path within the national forest. [1]

Upon entering Bibb County, the tornado moved through the community of Eoline, where the NWS survey rated the damage as EF3 with estimated winds of 145 mph, before the tornado weakened to EF2 intensity as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton and finally dissipated just northeast of Marvel. [1]

title: Impacts
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado caused 7 fatalities and 50 injuries along its 72.13-mile path through Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, according to the NWS Birmingham survey. [1]

In Hale County, particularly in and near the community of Sawyerville, the tornado produced extensive structural damage as it crossed Alabama Route 14 and nearby roads, destroying numerous mobile homes and single-family residences as well as at least one church, and downing thousands of trees. The survey attributes roughly 40 injuries and 6 of the 7 total fatalities to this portion of the track. [1]

Within the Talladega National Forest, the tornado caused widespread tree damage, with the NWS survey describing significant tree loss along its path in the forested areas of Hale and Bibb counties. [1]

In Bibb County, the tornado inflicted severe damage in the Eoline area, where numerous mobile homes and single-family houses sustained minor to major damage and about a dozen such structures were destroyed. The tornado also demolished the Eoline Fire Department building and another business. One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire department, and at least 10 additional injuries were reported in this segment of the path. [1]

After leaving Eoline and crossing Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, the tornado, then rated EF2 with estimated winds of about 125 mph, continued to damage or destroy several mobile homes and single-family residences near County Road 26 before weakening and lifting near Marvel; along the later portions of the path, thousands of additional trees were reported downed. [1]

title: Context within the April 27, 2011 outbreak
content:
The NWS Mobile/Pensacola office notes that the April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak produced a total of 343 tornadoes across the United States, including approximately 207 tornadoes on April 27 alone, and that four of the April 27 tornadoes reached EF5 intensity, underscoring the scale and severity of the event in which the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred. [3]

Within Alabama, the outbreak affected multiple National Weather Service County Warning Areas, with the NWS Mobile/Pensacola office documenting that only one of the 207 April 27 tornadoes occurred in its jurisdiction—an EF3 tornado in Choctaw County whose track spanned three different warning areas—while numerous other tornadoes, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, were documented by the NWS Birmingham office in central Alabama. [2][3]
